In [[group representation theory]], a branch of mathematics, '''Artin's theorem on induced characters''', introduced by [[E. Artin]], states that a [[Character_theory#Definitions|character]] on a [[finite group]] is a rational [[linear combination]] of [[induced character|characters induced]] from all [[cyclic group|cyclic]] [[subgroups]] of the group.

There is a similar but in some sense more precise [[Brauer's theorem on induced characters|theorem due to Brauer]], which says that the theorem remains true if "rational" and "cyclic subgroup" are replaced with "integer" and "[[elementary group|elementary subgroup]]".

== Statement ==
In ''Linear Representation of Finite Groups'' [[Jean-Pierre Serre|Serre]] states in Chapter 9.2, 17 <ref>{{Cite book |last=Serre |first=Jean-Pierre |title=Linear Representations of Finite Groups |date=1977 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-1-4684-9458-7 |location=New York, NY |oclc=853264255}}</ref> the theorem in the following, more general way:

Let <math>G</math> be a finite group and <math>X</math> any family of subgroups.

Then the following are equivalent:

# <math>G</math> is the union of conjugates of the subgroups in <math>X</math>: <math>G = \bigcup_{g\in G, H \in X} g^{-1}Hg</math>
# for every character <math>\chi</math> of <math>G</math> there exist characters <math>\chi_H</math> of <math>H</math> for each <math>H \in X</math> and <math>n \in \N</math> such that <math>n \chi = \sum_{H\in X} \text{Ind}_H^G(\chi_H)</math>

This in turn implies Artin's original statement, by choosing <math>X</math> to be the set of all [[Cyclic group|cyclic]] subgroups of <math>G</math>.

== Proof ==
Let <math>G</math> be a finite group and <math>(\chi_i)</math> its irreducible characters. Recall the [[representation ring]] <math>\mathcal{R}(G)</math> is the [[free abelian group]] on the set <math>\{\chi_i\}</math>.  Since all of <math>G</math>'s characters are linear combinations of <math>(\chi_i)</math> with nonnegative integer coefficients, every element of <math>\mathcal{R}(G)</math> is the difference of two characters of <math>G</math>.  Moreover, because the product of two characters is also a character, <math>\mathcal{R}(G)</math> is a ring.  It is a sub-ring of the <math>\mathbb{C}</math>-algebra of [[class function|class functions]] on <math>G</math>.  This algebra is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{C}\otimes\mathcal{R}(G)</math>, and has <math>(\chi_i)</math> as a basis.

Both the operation <math>\text{Res}</math> of restricting a representation of <math>G</math> to one of its subgroups <math>H</math> and the adjoint operation <math>\text{Ind}</math> of [[induced representation|inducing]] representations from <math>H</math> to <math>G</math> give abelian group homomorphisms:

<math>\begin{array}{cccl} \text{Res} \colon & \mathcal{R}(G) &\to& \mathcal{R}(H) \\ & \sum k_i\chi_i &\mapsto& \sum k_i \text{Res}_H^G \chi_i \end{array}</math>

<math>\begin{array}{cccl} \text{Ind} \colon & \mathcal{R}(H) &\to& \,\mathcal{R}(G) \\  & \sum k_i\chi_i &\mapsto& \sum k_i \text{Ind}_H^G \chi_i \end{array} </math>

where <math>\text{Res}</math> is actually a [[ring homomorphism]].

With these notations, the theorem can be equivalently rewritten as follows.  If <math>X</math> is a family of subgroups of <math>G</math>, the following properties are equivalent:
# <math>G</math> is the union of the conjugates of the subgroups in <math>X</math>
# The [[cokernel]] of <math>\text{Ind} \colon \bigoplus_{H\in X}\mathcal{R}(H) \to \mathcal{R}(G)</math> is finite.

We start with the following lemma:

'''Lemma.''' Let <math>H</math> be an element of <math>X</math>.  We claim that for every <math>f\in\mathcal{R}(H)</math>, <math>\text{Ind}(f)</math> vanishes on <math>g\in G</math> if <math>g</math> is not conjugate to any <math>h \in H</math>.

'''Proof.''' It is enough to prove this lemma for the character <math>\phi</math> of a representation <math>\theta \colon H\to \mathrm{GL}(W)</math>, since any <math>f \in\mathcal{R}(H)</math> is a difference of two such characters.  So, let <math>\rho \colon G\to \mathrm{GL}(V)</math> be the representation of <math>G</math> induced from the representation <math>\theta</math> of <math>H</math>, and let  <math>(r_i)</math> be a set of representatives of the cosets of <math>H</math> in <math>G</math>, which are the points of <math>G/H</math>. By definition of [[induced representation]], <math>V</math> is the direct sum of its subspaces <math>\rho(r_i) W</math>, and the linear transformation <math>\rho(g)</math> permutes these subspaces, since 

:: <math>\rho(g) \circ \rho(r_i)W=\rho(g r_i) W=\rho(r_{i'})W</math> 

where <math>g r_i=r_{i'}h</math> for some <math>h\in H</math>. To show that <math>\text{Ind}(\phi)(g)=\text{tr}_V(\rho(g))</math> vanishes, we now choose a basis for <math>V</math> that is a union of the bases of the subspaces <math>\rho(r_i)W</math>.  In this basis for <math>V</math>, the [[diagonal matrix]] entry of <math>\rho(g)</math> vanishes for each basis vector in <math>\rho(r_i)W</math> with <math>r_i\neq r_{i'}</math>.  But <math>r_i=r_{i'}</math> would imply <math>r_i^{-1} g r_i = h \in H</math>, which is ruled out by our assumption that <math>g</math> is not conjugate to any element of <math>H</math>.  Thus, all the diagonal matrix entries of <math>\rho(g)</math> vanish, so <math>\text{tr}_V(\rho_g)=0</math> as desired, proving the lemma.   ■

Now we prove 2. <math>\implies</math> 1.   The lemma implies that all elements in the image of <math>\text{Ind} \colon \bigoplus_{H\in X}\mathcal{R}(H) \to \mathcal{R}(G)</math> vanish on every <math>g \in G</math> in 

:: <math>S:= G - \bigcup_{g\in G, H \in X} g^{-1}Hg</math>, 

The same therefore holds for all elements in the image of the <math>\mathbb{C}</math>-linear map 

: <math>\mathbb{C}\otimes \text{Ind} \colon \mathbb{C}\otimes\bigoplus_{H\in X}\mathcal{R}(H) \to \mathbb{C}\otimes\mathcal{R}(G)</math> 

On the other hand, this map is surjective, because otherwise <math>\text{Ind}</math> would have an infinite cokernel, contradicting assumption 2.  Thus, every element of <math>\mathbb{C}\otimes\mathcal{R}(G)</math> vanishes on  <math>S</math>, insuring <math>S= \emptyset</math>, so that every element of <math>G</math> is conjugate to an element of some subgroup <math>H \in X</math>, as was to be shown.

Let us now prove 1. <math>\implies</math> 2.
First, note that it is enough to show 1. implies that
<math>\mathbb{C}\otimes \text{Ind}\colon \mathbb{C}\otimes\bigoplus_{H\in X}\mathcal{R}(H) \to \mathbb{C}\otimes\mathcal{R}(G)</math>
is surjective.  Indeed, this surjectivity implies that <math>\mathbb{C}\otimes\mathcal{R}(G)</math> has a basis <math>(e_i)</math> composed of elements of the image <math>A</math> of <math>\text{Ind}</math>.  Since this basis must have the same cardinality <math>n</math> as <math>(\chi_i)</math>, the quotient <math>\mathcal{R}(G)/A</math> is isomorphic to some quotient <math>\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod_i^n H_i\cong \prod_i^n\mathbb{Z}/H_i</math> where the <math>H_i</math> are non-trivial ideals of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, and this quotient is clearly finite, giving 2.

By duality, proving the surjectivity of <math>\mathbb{C}\otimes \text{Ind}</math> is equivalent to proving the injectivity of

: <math>\mathbb{C}\otimes \text{Res}\colon \mathbb{C}\otimes\mathcal{R}(G) \to \mathbb{C}\otimes\bigoplus_{H\in X}\mathcal{R}(H).</math> 
However, this is clearly true, because it is equivalent to saying that if a character vanishes on every [[conjugacy class]] of <math>G</math> it vanishes, which holds because characters are constant on each conjugacy class.

This concludes the proof of the theorem.
